body: In order to gain access to Native land
through its privatization as property,
colonizers
further
maintained their claim to power over Native peoples and their land by securing positions of superiority through the exploitation of Black bodies
Though settler colonialism and anti-Blackness constitute different logics, they are also deeply entangled
Both settler-colonial power and anti-Black racism maintain ongoing social orders and methods of domination
in the United States (King, 2013, p. 3).
Settler colonialism is a structure rather than an event
(Wolfe, 2006, p. 388). Therefore,
settler colonialism demands the continual exploitation of racialized Others to extract
value
from Indigenous
people’s
land and
the privatization of its
resources

. For example, landless European settlers secured their self-imposed right to Native land by driving cattle off Cherokee land and obtaining its cotton by Black slave labor (p. 392). Settler colonialism is as an ongoing project and thus, in order to further obtain control over their privatization of land and its economic resources, colonizers developed blood quantum rules to determine racialized regimes.
While non-Indian ancestry compromised Native people’s Indigeneity, having any amount of African ancestry made a person Black, regardless of phenotypical appearance

Although their racialization was determined through oppositional logics, their racialized renderings were both strategically determined in order to develop and maintain specific roles in order to bolster the
United States
nation state

. The role of Indigenous peoples within this system was one which was predicated on eliminating the Native to obtain and claim the title of the original owner of land. Conversely Black people were placed into the role of slave because their reproduction accrued wealth (pp. 387-388).
Moreover, settler colonialism relies upon the continual accumulation of land as private property.
A tactic used to render Native land as
private
property is the imposition and continual institutionalization of Western gender orders, heteropatriarchal arrangements, and racialized sexuality, which consequently accompanied sexual violence
Indigenous feminist analytics
certainly
draw out this tactic in
their analytics of
settler colonialism and sexual violence
They do so by outlining the ways in which
settler colonialism has long relied upon
the ongoing accumulation of Native land through
Western conceptualizations of gender and heteropatriarchal governance, which allows for the gendered Native female body to be othered and exterminated
(pp. 6-7). For instance, Native feminists have pointed out that the ways in which
settler colonialism continues to
operate is the naturalization of heteropatriarchy and heteropaternalism, which
organize
s the
social relations of citizens into nuclear families, of which they are expected to express “proper modern sexuality”
(Arvin, Tuck, & Morrill, 2013, pp. 14-15). Due the fact that these features of settler colonialism bolster and support the United States nation state,
settler nations rely upon the eradication and remaking of Indigenous people’s traditional governmental structures, gender roles, sexuality, and kinship
These processes have a long history of accompanying the routine abuse and sexual violence of Native women. Thus, sexual violence is a historical tool of settler colonialism.
Moreover, because settler colonialism is a structure rather than an event, (Wolfe, 2006, p. 388
), sexual violence is a weapon used to make settler colonialism an ongoing structure of permanence.
Black feminist theorizations of sexual violence converge with Indigenous feminist theorizations of sexual violence because they both note the ways in which
sexual violence keeps the
United States
nation state alive and in control of the physical and material lives
of whom its subjects render their Others
. King (2013) explains that
Black feminist thought allowed
her
to think about how gender has functioned as an ideal symbol of spatialized expansion
(pp. 14-15). Through the ongoing accrual of land,
the material bodies of Black women allow settlers to inhabit Indigenous land and “self-actualize”
(pp. 6-7). Povinelli (2006) illustrates
that processes of self-actualization are integral to colonial projects
, as the
colonial conceptualization
of European Enlightenment
granted the Western white male the ability to name themselves and other
s, ultimately
placing him in a position of superiority over racialized Others

(p. 184). Furthermore, in order to keep in control of Indigenous land, settlers named themselves the original owners of Native land through the routine rape of Black women, which much like Native land, were rendered as white male property.
